answer: The warning happens because you're calling my_channel.send(...) from callbacks that run on threads other than the one running your asyncio event loop. on_open() fires inside the aiohttp/aiortc loop (started via web.run_app in one asyncio.to_thread thread), but on_frame_arrived is invoked by windows-capture's own capture thread, a completely different OS thread with no running loop. aiortc's send/internal transport methods rely on the event loop (call_soon/ensure_future); when invoked from a foreign thread, a coroutine/future gets created but never scheduled on the loop that owns it, producing 'was never awaited'. Fix: capture the aiortc loop object (loop = asyncio.get_event_loop() inside offer()/main(), store it globally), then from on_frame_arrived marshal the send onto that loop instead of calling it directly: asyncio.run_coroutine_threadsafe(coro, loop) for coroutines, or loop.call_soon_threadsafe(my_channel.send, data) if send itself is synchronous. Never touch aiortc objects directly from a thread that doesn't own their event loop.

pystray issues on 3.13 are often just a stale/incompatible install (it depends on Pillow and platform backends), first try: pip install --upgrade pystray pillow, and confirm you have the right backend for your OS (pywin32 on Windows). If it still doesn't work, alternatives for a Windows system-tray icon: (1) PyQt5/PySide6's QSystemTrayIcon, the most full-featured and actively maintained option; (2) wxPython's wx.adv.TaskBarIcon; (3) raw pywin32, building the tray icon yourself with shell_notifyicon/win32gui, more code but no extra heavy GUI dependency; (4) infi.systray, lightweight and Windows-only but less actively maintained so may hit similar version issues. For a Tkinter-based app, PyQt/wx pull in a second GUI toolkit just for the tray icon, so pywin32's low-level API is often the least invasive choice if you want to stay dependency-light. Also check the project's GitHub issues, a popular tray library like pystray likely already has an open issue or PR about 3.13 compatibility.

Your IniVisitor methods (visit_expr, visit_entry, visit_section, visit_pair) don't match any rule name in pts_grammar, whose rules are top, tagline, taginact, tagenc, par1, charset, hm, word, ws, anytext, emptyline. Those visitor method names come from the parsimonious PyPI tutorial's different grammar (which defines expr/entry/section/pair rules). Parsimonious calls 'visit_' + rule_name for each node as it walks the tree, so visit_expr/visit_entry/etc. simply never fire against your grammar, everything falls through to generic_visit, which just returns nested lists of Node objects/text instead of a clean dict. Fix: either rewrite your grammar's rule names to match the tutorial (expr/entry/section/key/value), or write visitor methods matching your actual rules, e.g. visit_top, visit_tagline, visit_taginact, visit_tagenc, visit_par1, visit_charset, visit_word, each returning the structured piece you want, then combine in visit_tagline and accumulate in visit_top. Grammar and visitor must share rule names 1:1 for the NodeVisitor dispatch to do anything beyond generic_visit.

API Gateway's nameQuery only supports a 'starts with' prefix match server-side, there's no negation/NOT operator in the underlying REST API, so boto3's get_api_keys(nameQuery=...) can't express 'does not match'. None of !prefix-, NOT prefix-, ~prefix- are supported syntax, they're just treated as literal prefixes matching nothing, since no key name starts with those characters. The only way to exclude keys with a given prefix is to fetch all keys (paginate, without nameQuery) and filter client-side in Python: get a paginator via client.get_paginator('get_api_keys'), iterate paginator.paginate(includeValues=False), and keep only items where not item['name'].startswith('prefix-'). This applies to every AWS SDK since they all just wrap the same underlying API Gateway REST endpoint and its nameQuery parameter, there is no richer server-side filtering available.

Langflow uploaded chat files are managed through its internal StorageService abstraction, not a fixed OS path you should hardcode, that's why the same relative name resolves to /app/... on Datastax (container filesystem/mounted volume) and C:/Data/... locally, and why direct PIL Image.open(filename) fails in both. Instead of building a path yourself, use the storage service Langflow injects/exposes to components to fetch the file by flow_id (or session id) plus file name, via the component's access to self.graph/self.vertex context or the documented file-handling helpers for custom components, which return bytes you can feed into Image.open(io.BytesIO(data)) or send directly to the API call, this works the same whether the backend is local disk or Datastax's managed storage. Because this depends on your exact Langflow version's internal API, check that version's Files / custom component docs or the StorageService source for the exact method name if a ready-made helper isn't available in your build.

Use plain .py files, not more notebooks, for your calculation sub-modules. Put reusable functions/classes into a small local package (e.g., a src/ or lib/ folder with .py files), import them into your main notebook normally (from mymodule import my_func), and enable autoreload so edits are picked up without restarting the kernel by running %load_ext autoreload followed by %autoreload 2 in a notebook cell. Keep the notebook itself as the thin interactive/orchestration layer, calling functions, inspecting results, plotting, while the actual pandas/numpy/statsmodels logic lives in testable, version-control-friendly .py modules. This gives you real Python imports, IDE navigation/refactoring, unit tests via pytest, and cleaner diffs, none of which you get from splitting logic across multiple .ipynb files, which requires slower and more fragile mechanisms like %run other.ipynb, papermill, or nbclient just to reuse code. Reserve extra notebooks for genuinely separate exploratory analyses, not reusable calculation code.

Without the actual error text it's hard to pin down exactly, but loading an old .h5 Keras file on a newer TF/Keras usually fails for one of these reasons: (1) optimizer-state deserialization, try keras.models.load_model('model.h5', compile=False) first since you likely only need inference; (2) custom layers/losses/metrics not registered, pass custom_objects={'Name': cls} if the model used any; (3) if you're on Keras 3 (bundled with TF 2.16+), legacy H5 files can need the compatibility shim, pip install tf-keras and set TF_USE_LEGACY_KERAS=1 before importing TensorFlow; (4) verify the file isn't corrupted or truncated by opening it directly with h5py.File(path,'r') and checking attrs like keras_version; (5) if it was saved with a much older TF1.x/standalone Keras, you may need an environment with a closer-matching TF version to load it once, then re-save in the modern .keras/SavedModel format for future compatibility.

BaseHTTPMiddleware always wraps the endpoint's real response in Starlette's internal _StreamingResponse, that's just how it plumbs the ASGI send channel through call_next(). It reconstructs a streaming-style response from the raw http.response.start/body messages regardless of whether your route returned Response, JSONResponse, or StreamingResponse, so the original response class is genuinely lost by the time dispatch() sees it, you can't reliably isinstance()-check it back into the original type. Practical alternatives: (1) don't use BaseHTTPMiddleware for this, write pure ASGI middleware (a class wrapping app.__call__(scope, receive, send)) so you can inspect the raw messages and know exactly when the body is fully sent, closing the session there; (2) have streaming endpoints explicitly set request.state.is_streaming = True or a custom response header, and check that in dispatch instead of type(response); (3) close the DB session inside the streaming generator itself in a finally block, which sidesteps the detection problem entirely.

The bug is this line: command=filter_data(sql). Since command expects a callable reference, writing filter_data(sql) instead calls the function immediately, once, while the button is being built, using whatever sql/entry_value.get() evaluates to at that moment (almost certainly an empty string, since the user hasn't typed anything yet), and binds the button's command to filter_data's return value (df2, not a function), so clicking the button does nothing afterward. That's why display_data(dataf) sees dataf is None, sqldf on an empty/invalid query returns None or errors. Fix: wrap it in a lambda so it runs on click and reads the entry live: command=lambda: filter_data(entry_value.get()) instead of command=filter_data(sql). Also update the global df inside filter_data (df = df2) if later queries should operate on the filtered result, and wrap sqldf() in try/except to handle invalid SQL gracefully instead of returning None silently.

This is a known regression tied to Python 3.13's new PyREPL, the rewritten interactive interpreter that replaced the old readline-based REPL. The new REPL does its own auto-indentation/bracket handling, and in some terminals (including Windows Terminal) it doesn't always detect pasted multi-line text as a single paste, so it applies its own auto-indent on top of the pasted lines' existing indentation, effectively doubling it. Workarounds: (1) set the environment variable PYTHON_BASIC_REPL=1 before launching Python to fall back to the old, non-PyREPL interactive shell, which doesn't have this behavior; (2) avoid interactive paste altogether, save the code to a .py file and run it with python script.py; (3) update to the latest 3.13.x patch, since PyREPL paste-handling bugs were actively being fixed post-3.13.0/3.13.1; (4) check Windows Terminal's bracketed-paste support. Search the CPython issue tracker for PyREPL plus paste plus indentation for the exact tracked bug and its status.

For a finite, well-understood set of failure categories (connectivity, disk space, memory, timeouts), you likely don't need NLP/ML at all, a rule-based, config-driven matcher is simpler, deterministic, auditable, and far easier to justify for auto-remediating production jobs than a black-box model. Build a prioritized table of regex pattern or fuzzy-match signature to remediation action, match each incoming error message against it in order (Python re, or rapidfuzz/thefuzz if wording varies slightly), execute the first matching action, and explicitly fall back to 'no automated action, escalate to human' for anything unmatched, logging every match and decision for audit. Reserve NLP/embedding-similarity approaches for cases where messages are too free-form for fixed patterns to keep up, and even then use ML to suggest or rank candidate rules rather than to autonomously trigger remediation. Look into AIOps / runbook-automation literature and tools (e.g. Rundeck, StackStorm) for prior architectures of exactly this pattern.

Two separate issues here. First, fbprophet is the old, unmaintained package name, the current one is prophet (pip install prophet or conda install -c conda-forge prophet), with from prophet import Prophet; fbprophet's dependency chain (old pystan) is broken on modern Python/NumPy, a likely direct cause of import-time errors. Second, and more telling: you said even python -V fails with the same error, that can't be caused by fbprophet at all, since -V doesn't execute any user code or imports; it means your interpreter/environment itself is broken (corrupted conda env, a bad PYTHONPATH or PYTHONSTARTUP pointing at broken code, or a broken spyder-kernels install shimming all invocations). Fix the environment first: unset/check PYTHONPATH and PYTHONSTARTUP, and run python -V from a plain terminal outside Spyder to isolate whether Spyder's kernel customization is the culprit. Then create a fresh conda env (Python 3.10/3.11, since old pystan-based fbprophet doesn't support 3.12) and install prophet there instead.

cmds.ls(sl=True) reflects the viewport/outliner selection, not the tool's internal influence selection. Query the Paint Skin Weights tool context directly instead: ctx = cmds.currentCtx(), then joint = cmds.artAttrSkinPaintCtx(ctx, query=True, influence=True). This returns the name of the currently highlighted influence/joint in the tool settings' influence tree, as long as the Paint Skin Weights tool is actually active (currentCtx() will be an artAttrSkinPaintCtx-type context in that case, worth checking before you query, to avoid errors if some other tool is active). This command and its influence flag is the standard way rigging tools read the active paint influence, and it has been stable across recent Maya versions including 2025.

In the Python v2 programming model, Azure Functions discovers all your functions by importing function_app.py, if that import raises any exception (missing package, bad decorator arguments, an unresolved trigger binding), indexing fails for the entire app and Azure shows zero functions, not just the broken trigger. Adding event_hub_message_trigger is almost certainly hitting one of: (1) azure-eventhub (and a current azure-functions version) missing from requirements.txt even though it works locally with it installed elsewhere; (2) the connection= value must be the NAME of an App Setting holding the Event Hub connection string/namespace, not the string itself, a missing or misnamed setting can break indexing on Flex Consumption; (3) an extension bundle version in host.json too old to support eventHub triggers. Don't rely on the Portal's silent 'no functions found', run func start locally with a valid local.settings.json to see the real Python traceback from indexing, which will point at the exact cause.

arr = [[]] * 2 creates a list holding two references to the exact same inner list object, multiplying a list with * replicates references, it does not deep-copy the elements. So arr[0] and arr[1] are literally the same object; appending to one appends to both, exactly what you observed. This is a classic Python pitfall, most commonly hit as [[]]*n or [0]*n, it only becomes visible with mutable elements like lists because appending mutates the shared object in place; with immutable elements like plain ints it looks fine, since arr[0] += 1 rebinds that slot to a new int rather than mutating a shared object. Fix: build independent lists with a comprehension instead of multiplication: arr = [[] for _ in range(2)]. Now each element is its own separate list object, and your partitioning loop will work as expected.

PyTorch 2.6 changed torch.load's weights_only default from False to True, which breaks loading Lightning/GluonTS checkpoints that pickle non-tensor objects (hyperparameters, optimizer state). Internally, DeepAREstimator.train() calls PyTorch Lightning's load_from_checkpoint, which calls torch.load without explicitly overriding weights_only, so under 2.6 it now fails where it silently worked before. Fixes, in order of preference: (1) upgrade gluonts and lightning/pytorch-lightning to their latest releases, this is a known break reported against several libraries and has been getting patched to pass weights_only=False explicitly; (2) pin PyTorch below 2.6 (pip install 'torch<2.6') until your installed gluonts/lightning versions are patched; (3) as a last-resort workaround, monkeypatch torch.load to default weights_only=False before calling .train(), only safe if you fully trust the checkpoint source, since that's exactly the protection the new default is meant to provide.

UnrecognizedClientException / security token invalid means the access key and secret you're passing are not being accepted as valid credentials, it's unrelated to having the AWS CLI or a ~/.aws/credentials file installed (boto3.Session with explicit aws_access_key_id/aws_secret_access_key doesn't need either). Most likely causes: (1) the access key was deleted, deactivated, or rotated in IAM and this pair no longer exists; (2) a copy-paste error, extra whitespace, a missing/truncated character, or accidentally swapping key id and secret; (3) these are actually temporary/STS credentials (e.g. from SSO or AssumeRole) that also require aws_session_token, omitting it with temporary creds produces exactly this error. Fix: generate a brand-new access key pair for an IAM user in the console, paste it carefully (or load from env vars instead of hardcoding), and confirm the IAM user/role has polly:SynthesizeSpeech permission once authentication succeeds. eu-north-1 is a standard, non-opt-in region so that's not the issue.

This looks like a known limitation of BlueZ's MPRIS-style MediaPlayer1 D-Bus interface rather than something fixable purely in your app's logic: the Position property is a snapshot, not something BlueZ reliably pushes via PropertiesChanged when it changes, many implementations exclude Position from change notifications since it changes continuously during normal playback, and after a seek/rewind the remote device's AVRCP response updating Position can lag or not arrive as a signal at all. So watching for signals won't reliably catch position jumps; you need to actively poll the Position property yourself (re-query org.bluez's MediaPlayer1.Position on a timer, e.g. every second) rather than expect qdbus6/bluez to notify you. Practically: after issuing any seek/prev/next control, wait briefly then explicitly re-read Position instead of trusting a signal, and interpolate locally between polls using a monotonic clock while Status is playing so the displayed position doesn't just keep counting from the stale value.

reasoning=None isn't a real parameter for controlling this, for GPT-5-family models the control is reasoning_effort, and for gpt-5-nano the lowest setting is 'minimal', which gets you closest to no reasoning (there currently isn't a full hard off-switch for reasoning models, minimal is as low as it goes). If you're using the Responses API, pass it as a nested object: reasoning={'effort': 'minimal'} in client.responses.create(...), not a bare reasoning=None kwarg on chat.completions.create, mixing up the two APIs/parameter shapes is the most likely reason it silently has no effect. Also check your SDK version is recent enough to support gpt-5's reasoning_effort parameter, older openai-python versions will just ignore or reject unknown kwargs. If minimal still isn't fast/cheap enough for your batch inference use case, gpt-4o-mini, a genuinely non-reasoning model, may remain the more predictable choice for a simple classification task like gender inference despite gpt-5-nano's lower list price.

Your reading is slightly off. The bare * doesn't collect positional args, that's what *args does, it just marks a boundary: every parameter after it becomes keyword-only, so object_list must be passed as object_list=value by callers, never positionally. There's no 'required positional unnamed arguments' involved. The = ... is an ordinary default value where the default happens to be Python's builtin Ellipsis singleton (the same object you get anywhere you write ... in code), it's not special syntax tied to *, just a sentinel meaning 'caller didn't explicitly supply this,' chosen instead of None because None might be a legitimate value someone wants to pass. The method body typically checks if object_list is ...: to detect the missing case and compute a real default at runtime. **kwargs then absorbs any other keyword arguments. So: an optional keyword-only object_list parameter defaulting to a distinguishable not-given sentinel, plus catch-all kwargs.
